items.definition: A form of English used by a particular group in a particular place, with its own vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation.
items.example: Singapore English is a variety of English, not a broken version of it.

items.definition: The way the sounds of a language are pronounced by a speaker, independent of which words they use.
items.example: He has a strong Glasgow accent but standard vocabulary.

items.definition: Whether a speaker pronounces the r sound at the end of a word. American English is rhotic; British English is not.
items.example: The difference between *car* and *cah* is rhoticity.

items.definition: The level of formality a speaker chooses for a situation, from casual to formal.
items.example: Switching register, he changed *Could you pass the salt* to *Pass the salt*.

items.definition: Moving between two languages, or two varieties of one language, inside a single conversation.
items.example: Code-switching between English and Tamil is normal in Chennai offices.

items.definition: A shared language used between people whose first languages differ. English is the most common one in international business.
items.example: English works as the lingua franca, so nobody has to learn three languages for one meeting.

items.definition: The individual version of a language: one speaker's own habits of words and grammar.
items.example: Every email you write becomes part of your idiolect.

items.definition: An unplanned stop in which the car cannot be driven safely. It is the stop, not the specific fault that caused it.
items.example: I have had a breakdown on the motorway, and I need a recovery vehicle.

items.definition: The service that comes to help a broken-down car. It comes through insurance, a manufacturer package or a separate membership.
items.example: Do you know whether my roadside assistance covers a call-out in this area?

items.definition: The van or truck sent to collect the car. Some can lift a car and some can only tow it on a wheel.
items.example: The recovery vehicle will lift the car, so I do not need to empty the boot.

items.definition: All four indicators blink together. The car is stationary or unusual. Severity level 1 — Information / Status. Action: Nothing to do while the lights are on. Switch them off once the car moves again..
The red reflective triangle placed on the road behind a stopped vehicle so drivers see it in time.
items.example: Put the warning triangle out about 100 metres behind the car.

items.definition: Starting a car with a flat battery by connecting it to the battery of another car with cables.
items.example: Could you send someone to jump start the car? The battery is flat.

items.definition: A unit of energy in food. One gram of fat holds about 9 kcal, a gram of carbohydrate or protein about 4.
items.example: This bar contains 250 kcal, which is about a tenth of a day's energy.

items.definition: The date after which the food is still safe to eat but has gone down in quality. A quality date, not a safety date.
items.example: The best-before date has passed, so the biscuits are only stale, not bad.

items.definition: The date after which the food may no longer be safe to eat. It is a safety date and it is not negotiable.
items.example: The use-by date was yesterday, so I threw the chicken away.

items.definition: The amount of the product the nutrition figures are given for. It is the maker's choice, so it often does not match what you eat.
items.example: One serving is 30 g, which is much less than the bowl I had.

items.definition: A substance in food that can cause a serious allergic reaction in some people. There are fourteen that have to be declared.
items.example: The allergen box says it contains peanuts and soya.

items.definition: The unbroken path a chilled product follows from the factory to your fridge. If the chain breaks, the use-by date stops meaning anything.
items.example: The cold chain was broken, so the date on the pack means nothing.

items.definition: To put something that has thawed back into the freezer. For meat and fish this is a safety question, not a quality one.
items.example: You can freeze it now, but you cannot refreeze it once it has thawed.

items.definition: The amount of the product the nutrition figures are given for. It is the maker's choice, so it often does not match what you eat.
items.example: One serving is 30 g, which is much less than the bowl I had.

items.definition: A daily guide for an average adult, used as the yardstick the percentages on a panel are measured against.
items.example: One portion gives me 40 % of the daily value for salt.

items.definition: The average daily amount of energy or a nutrient for an adult. A guide, not a target.
items.example: The reference intake for energy is about 2000 kilocalories a day.

items.definition: One of the three nutrients the body needs in quantity: carbohydrate, fat and protein.
items.example: The main macronutrient in this product is fat, not carbohydrate.

items.definition: The saturated fats, which are the part of the fat that matters most for blood cholesterol.
items.example: It has 11 g of saturates, which is over half the daily reference.

items.definition: Sugar the manufacturer added, as distinct from sugar that came with the fruit or the milk.
items.example: Total sugars are 20 g, and added sugars are 15 g of that.

items.definition: The element that makes salt salty. A label quoting salt is quoting sodium plus the chloride with it.
items.example: This has 0.5 g of sodium per 100 g, which is low.

items.definition: The roughly 24-hour cycle that sets your sleep, hormones, body temperature and appetite. Light is its strongest input.
items.example: My circadian rhythm has shifted, because I have been going to bed at two every night.

items.definition: The time between getting into bed and falling asleep. Under about twenty minutes is normal.
items.example: My sleep onset latency is about forty minutes, most nights.

items.definition: The share of your time in bed that you were actually asleep. A long night can still be an inefficient one.
items.example: I was in bed for nine hours and my sleep efficiency was about seventy per cent.

items.definition: The dreaming stage of sleep, when memory is consolidated and emotional reactions are regulated.
items.example: Alcohol takes away REM sleep, so I wake up tired even after a long night.

items.definition: The accumulated gap between the sleep you have had and the sleep you need. It can be partly repaid, but slowly.
items.example: I have been building up sleep debt for three weeks of early starts.

items.definition: Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, together with daytime impairment. The daytime effect is part of the definition.
items.example: It is not just that I sleep badly; it is that I cannot work properly the next day. That makes it insomnia.

items.definition: Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, usually with snoring and gasping. You usually cannot notice it yourself.
items.example: My partner says I stop breathing in my sleep, so I will ask about sleep apnoea.

items.definition: A machine with two wheels that you push with your feet. A good bicycle makes your legs feel like they have a strong friend.
items.example: His grandfather's bicycle was heavy and rusty, and Nam loved it.

items.definition: The flat part of a bicycle that your foot stands on. When you push the pedals, the wheels turn.
items.example: The pedals were stiff, so he pushed them three times.

items.definition: The flat part that helps a bird to lift into the air. On this bicycle, the wings are only paper, but they still lift.
items.example: The newspaper wings lifted when he rang the bell.

items.definition: The small metal thing on a bicycle that makes a sound when you press it. Nam's bell is old and a bit tired.
items.example: He pressed the bell three times before the wings moved.

items.definition: The flat top of a building. In the old quarter, the rooftops are close enough to almost touch.
items.example: They landed on the roof garden above the old house.

items.definition: A big old building with thick walls, made to keep people safe. Castles usually have towers and gates.
items.example: From her window, Hà could see the castle on the hill.
